findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Make clear that run_step only times out the wait, and put a real limit on the blocking call itself (a deadline on accounting_lock / interprocess_lock acquisition), or justify why stuck threads are acceptable given the offload executor's size
evidence: Plan: "runs it on a worker thread under asyncio.wait_for, and raises ReviewStepTimeout when the bound expires"
git_fetch.py:58-72 interprocess_lock → lock_kernel.take_blocking_exclusive (no timeout); cache.py:100-108 accounting_lock uses it
app.py:61-73 a single named offload ThreadPoolExecutor with the default size; config.py:87-95 already notes 'A blocked to_thread worker may survive coroutine cancellation'

Retrieved: CPython issue #87185 reports the to_thread thread 'is never cancelled and continues running forever despite the timeout error thrown'; dev.to write-up: wait_for(to_thread) times out 'your wait, not the work'
findings.finding: The plan claims that run_step gives each pre-LLM step 'its own timeout', but asyncio.wait_for over a worker thread only times out the wait. The thread keeps running, and that is documented Python behaviour. The diagnosed stall is a thread blocked in interprocess_lock → lock_kernel.take_blocking_exclusive, which has no deadline. Each step that times out therefore leaves a thread blocked for up to the whole 45-51 minute walk, held in the bot's own offload ThreadPoolExecutor (default size min(32, cpu+4)). The reconciler retries the review every cycle, adding another stuck thread each time. That can fill the executor, so later run_step calls, and every other to_thread call in app.py/reconcile.py, queue behind threads that never finish. Each stuck thread also counts as a live offload thread at shutdown. The usual way to make a blocking call actually stop is to put the limit on the blocking call itself: a lock acquire with a deadline (the repo's _store.lock already has timeout and attempt settings) or a killable subprocess. The plan does not consider either.
findings.location: Approach step 2 — review_steps.run_step; AC 'Each review step before the LLM call ... has its own timeout well under 1200 s'
scenarios: Before step 1's fix is deployed, or during any future stall on the same lock: every retry of a stalled review leaves one more thread blocked on accounting_lock. After a few cycles the executor is full and even existing_vote_check (a quick Gerrit call) times out in the queue, so reviews fail at the wrong stage and the logs point to the wrong step.
findings.suggested_fix: Add an optional deadline to interprocess_lock (poll lock_kernel.take_exclusive non-blocking with backoff until a deadline, then raise a timeout error) and have the snapshot step pass the step timeout, so the stuck thread actually returns. Write in run_step's docstring that wait_for times out the wait, not the work. Add a test where repeated step timeouts against a held lock must not leave more than N live offload threads.

findings.finding: With the lock released during the walk, a concurrent eviction can delete files or directories mid-walk. The plan does not say the walk tolerates FileNotFoundError or vanished entries, and no test covers eviction during the walk; only the 'published mid-walk' edge is tested.

findings.finding: The sweep's walk now runs without accounting_lock. The plan does not say how the walk tolerates eviction deleting files or directories under it mid-walk. Before, the lock guaranteed nothing was deleted during the walk; now a FileNotFoundError from stat/scandir inside `cache.distinct_bytes` could abort startup_sweep. The testing plan only covers 'an entry published mid-walk', not an eviction mid-walk.
scenarios: A container starts and the 45-51 min walk begins. A review's populate triggers eviction of an old ticket snapshot. The walk stats a file that has just been unlinked and raises, so the sweep crashes or leaves the debris/accounting state half-done at every container start.
findings.suggested_fix: In the walk, catch FileNotFoundError per entry and per file and mark the walk 'disturbed'. Then rely on the entry-set comparison (which will differ) to keep the incremental total. Add a Testing bullet: evict an entry while the patched distinct_bytes is paused; the sweep completes and the total equals the bytes on disk.

findings.finding: The plan puts every pre-LLM step under one new `run_step` timeout and abandoned-thread scheme, but 4 of the 5 steps already have their own time limits. Only the snapshot step (the lock wait the plan names as the root cause) has none. The plan never mentions the existing limits, so the shared wrapper adds a second, overlapping bound to steps that already end on their own. It also makes `ReviewScratch` cover thread abandonment for steps whose threads would otherwise stop by themselves.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Base ReviewScratch on _mcp_health._CountedHandoff (count at submission on the event loop, exactly-one-side release, skip a body that was abandoned before it started) and add a test for a step queued but not yet started at close
evidence: Plan: "on close the folder is removed at once if no step thread runs in it, else by the last thread as it returns; a step submitted after close raises ReviewAbandoned without running"

src/rebar/_mcp_health.py:264-299 _CountedHandoff: "The count is therefore taken on the event loop before handoff ... Exactly one side releases it: the worker once the body ends, or the abandoning caller if the worker never started, in which case the body is skipped"
Absence: the plan does not mention _CountedHandoff or any existing handoff/refcount helper
findings.finding: ReviewScratch (Approach step 5) builds a new start/abandon handshake between a coroutine and its worker thread. The repo already has a reviewed version of this, _mcp_health._CountedHandoff, which fixed a real race (leprous-uncivic-crab), and the plan neither reuses it nor mentions it. The plan's rules also leave the same gap that bug exposed: close removes the folder 'if no step thread runs in it', and only a step 'submitted after close' is refused. A step submitted before close that is still queued in the executor (accepted, not yet running) is not covered. close sees no running thread and removes the folder, then the queued thread starts in a folder that no longer exists. That reproduces the 'reviewbot-… No such file' symptom this plan is trying to remove.
scenarios: The offload executor is saturated by step threads stuck on the lock. A new snapshot step is submitted and waits in the queue, the review is cancelled, ReviewScratch.close sees zero running threads and deletes the folder, and then the queued step runs against the missing path.
findings.suggested_fix: Count each step when it is submitted (on the loop, before run_in_executor), not when it starts running. Use the same queued/running/abandoned states as _CountedHandoff: close marks every still-queued handoff abandoned, and the folder is removed when the count reaches zero, whether by close or by the last running thread. Better still, move _CountedHandoff into a shared module and use it from both places.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify in Approach step 2 which threads run steps (a dedicated per-step thread or a separate bounded executor, not the shared reviewbot-offload pool), log the step start from inside the worker when it actually begins (plus a 'queued' line if needed), and log the count of abandoned step threads.
evidence: Plan: 'logs one INFO review_step line ... before the step starts, runs it on a worker thread under asyncio.wait_for'
app.py:68-73 installs ThreadPoolExecutor(thread_name_prefix='reviewbot-offload') with default max_workers as the loop's default executor
app.py:61-63: 'A cancelled to_thread coroutine can leave a non-daemon review thread running'
findings.finding: run_step says only 'runs it on a worker thread'. If that is asyncio.to_thread, every timed-out step leaves a thread stuck in the app's single shared offload pool (a ThreadPoolExecutor with default max_workers, installed by _install_offload_executor). Retries on the same stuck resource add more. Once the pool is full, every to_thread call (the worker's _superseded_by, Gerrit calls, artifact emission, new steps) waits in the queue. The INFO 'review_step' line is logged before the step actually starts, so a step that timed out while still queued is reported as stuck in a step it never ran. That defeats the attribution that AC1/AC2 depend on.
scenarios: An unidentified stall (e.g. git maintenance contention) affects clone: each 300 s timeout leaves one more thread stuck until the pool is full, then every review times out at its first step with a misleading step name
findings.suggested_fix: Run each step on its own named thread (prefix 'reviewbot-offload-step-', non-daemon so the shutdown force-exit gate still sees it) that sets a concurrent future, and await it with asyncio.wait_for(asyncio.wrap_future(fut), timeout). Emit review_step from inside the thread at entry, and emit review_step_abandoned with the current abandoned-thread count on timeout.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify the executor for run_step (a dedicated pool with stated size and daemon threads, or a thread per step), how a timed-out step's git subprocess is terminated, and that abandoned threads do not block process exit; add a test that a timed-out step does not keep the executor or interpreter shutdown blocked.
evidence: "runs it on a worker thread under `asyncio.wait_for`, and raises `ReviewStepTimeout` when the bound expires"
Context: "Each recreate then waits out the 1260 s stop grace period"
No mention of executor sizing, daemon threads, or killing a timed-out step's subprocess.
findings.finding: `run_step` runs each step on a worker thread under `asyncio.wait_for`. On timeout the thread (and any git subprocess) keeps running and cannot be cancelled. The plan does not say which executor is used, whether threads are daemon, or how stuck threads affect shutdown. Executor threads are joined at interpreter exit, so a thread blocked on the lock or a hung git call can hold the container through the 1260 s stop grace the Context names as a cause of the cycle. Stuck threads in a bounded default executor can also starve later steps: they queue, log their start line, then time out without running.
scenarios: A clone hangs behind git maintenance, the step times out, the git process and thread stay alive, and the next deploy's container stop waits the full grace period.
Repeated retries leak threads until the default executor is full, and every later review times out in its first step.
findings.suggested_fix: Use daemon threads (one per step) or a dedicated executor whose shutdown uses cancel_futures and wait=False; for clone/commit_fetch/diff_fetch pass the step deadline to subprocess timeout= so git is killed; log the start line only when the thread actually begins.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State in Approach how ReviewAbandoned is handled (e.g. caught in review_and_vote, logged at DEBUG, no VOTER_ERROR or vote) and define in step 4 what 'non-clone folder' means and that prepare_review_snapshot returns early for it.
evidence: "a step submitted after close raises `ReviewAbandoned` without running"
"`review_and_vote` turns `ReviewStepTimeout` into one `VOTER_ERROR`..." (no mention of ReviewAbandoned)
Testing: "a non-clone folder is skipped" with no counterpart in Approach step 4
findings.finding: Approach step 5 introduces `ReviewAbandoned` for steps submitted after close, but step 3 only says how `review_and_vote` handles `ReviewStepTimeout`. Whether ReviewAbandoned is logged, swallowed or surfaced, and what status it returns, is unstated. Testing also asserts 'a non-clone folder is skipped' for the snapshot pre-step, but the Approach does not define what a non-clone folder is or the skip behaviour.
scenarios: A cancelled review raises ReviewAbandoned, which propagates as an unhandled exception and logs a traceback, or is reported as a VOTER_ERROR and double-counted.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify the executor used by run_step (dedicated, sized), how abandoned step threads are bounded or reaped (e.g. kill the git subprocess on timeout), and log the step start from inside the worker thread so queue wait is distinguishable from step execution.
evidence: "runs it on a worker thread under `asyncio.wait_for`, and raises `ReviewStepTimeout` when the bound expires"
"removed ... by the last thread as it returns" (acknowledges threads outlive the timeout)
findings.finding: run_step runs each step on a worker thread under asyncio.wait_for. The timeout abandons the thread but does not stop it, so a hung clone or a blocked snapshot build keeps running (and keeps any git subprocess or lock it holds). The plan sets no bound on abandoned threads and does not name the executor. If abandoned threads fill a shared or default executor, later steps queue and hit their 300 s timeout without ever starting. The 'review_step' start line, logged before submission, then misattributes the stall to a step that never ran. The retry also launches a second snapshot build for the same SHA alongside the abandoned one.
scenarios: During a 45-min stall window, each retry abandons another snapshot thread blocked on the lock. After N retries the executor is full, every step times out in the queue, and the journal shows misleading 'review_step clone' starts with no progress.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Rewrite the Context's 'cause is not identified / hypotheses to test' paragraph as history, and state which hypotheses the investigation ruled out and which (e.g. git maintenance) are out of scope.
evidence: "The cause of the stall is not identified. Hypotheses to test: waiting on the tickets-store lock; clone or snapshot I/O stuck behind git maintenance; a step before the LLM call stuck with no timeout."
"Root cause (evidence: investigation comment on this ticket): `janitor.startup_sweep` holds the snapshot store's `accounting_lock`..."
findings.finding: The Context section says the stall's cause is not identified and lists hypotheses to test, while the Root cause section states the cause with evidence. The executor gets two signals: investigate three hypotheses, or implement the named fix.
scenarios: An implementer spends time testing the git-maintenance hypothesis, which the Root cause section already rules out or never addresses.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the paragraph with: 'Initial hypotheses were X, Y, Z; the investigation (comment on this ticket) found the startup_sweep lock hold; git-maintenance timeouts are out of scope for this ticket.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Make the sweep's reconciliation effective under concurrent traffic (e.g. per-entry byte reconciliation for unchanged entries plus a delta for changed ones), or explicitly accept the skip and log an INFO line when the reset is skipped so drift is observable.
evidence: "the walk takes 45-51 minutes (316 ticket snapshots of ~224,000 files)"
"reset the byte total only if the entry set is unchanged. Otherwise ... keep the incremental total."
findings.finding: The reset applies only if the entry set is unchanged across a walk that takes 45-51 minutes on the box, while reviews keep publishing snapshots. In production the set will almost always have changed, so the drift correction (the sweep's purpose) effectively never runs. The plan also does not say whether entry-set equality must cover name+inode reuse after an evict-then-repopulate.
scenarios: The incremental total has drifted (the reason the sweep reconciles), a review publishes during the walk, the reset is skipped, and the drift persists until the next container start, which also sees traffic.
findings.suggested_fix: Record per-entry bytes from the walk; under the re-taken lock, reset total = sum(walked bytes for entries whose name+inode is unchanged) + current incremental contribution of new or changed entries; log `startup_sweep_reconcile` with applied/skipped and the delta.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Replace (or supplement) the name+inode comparison with a mutation generation counter that is bumped under accounting_lock on every populate/evict, and reset the total only if the generation is unchanged.
evidence: "record the entry set (name + directory inode) in the same hold"
"reset the byte total only if the entry set is unchanged"
findings.finding: The 'entry set unchanged' check compares name + directory inode. If an entry is evicted and a same-name entry republished during the 45-51 min walk, and the filesystem reuses the inode number (ext4 readily does), this ABA case passes the check. The sweep then overwrites the correct incremental total with the walk's stale measurement.
scenarios: During the walk, entry X is evicted and then re-snapshotted under the same name; the new directory receives the freed inode. The comparison says 'unchanged', and a total computed from the old hardlink layout replaces the correct incremental total.
findings.suggested_fix: Keep a monotonically increasing `generation` in the store accounting, incremented under accounting_lock by every populate and eviction. startup_sweep records it in the first hold and resets the total only if it is equal at re-take.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Name a counted mechanism this plan retires, or add one sentence stating why ReviewScratch's threading.Lock cannot be avoided and why no retirement is possible.
evidence: "Its `threading.Lock` carries a `# mechanism-ok: lock` marker."
findings.finding: The plan adds a counted `lock` mechanism, the `threading.Lock` in `review_steps.ReviewScratch`. It names no retirement of any counted kind and gives no reason none is possible. Narrowing accounting_lock's hold does not retire a lock. A `# mechanism-ok: lock` marker is a suppression marker, not a stated justification in the plan.
scenarios: lock: ReviewScratch's threading.Lock (scratch-folder close vs. step-thread refcount)

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Back up or correct the 'gate then hits the cache' claim in step 4 for the ticket-store snapshot, e.g. pass the pre-step's resolved handle (code sha + tickets_path) to the gate, or call the gate with fetch=False after the pre-step, so the gate cannot re-pin and build a new tickets-<sha> outside the bounded snapshot step.
evidence: Plan: "calls gate_source.resolve_gate_handle(ref=\"HEAD\", source=None, repo_root=...), the gate's own first call (CodeReviewRequest defaults), so the gate then hits the cache."
src/rebar/llm/gate_source.py:152-155: `if handle.source == SOURCE_ATTESTED and materialize_ticket_store: handle = attach_materialized_tickets(handle, repo_root=repo_root, fetch=fetch, ...)`
src/rebar/_snapshot/repo_snapshot.py:617-640: materialize_tickets re-pins the tickets sha (fetch=True) and returns a cached entry only `if dest.is_dir()`.
src/rebar/_snapshot/repo_snapshot.py:651: comment "Fast-moving ticket tips rarely hit cache, so reuse a hardlinked neighbour"
Plan Root cause: "316 ticket snapshots of ~224,000 files"
findings.finding: Step 4's claim that the snapshot pre-step makes 'the gate then hits the cache' does not hold for the ticket-store half of the handle. resolve_gate_handle, by default (materialize_ticket_store=True, fetch=True), calls attach_materialized_tickets → materialize_tickets, which fetches again and pins the current tickets tip. A cache hit only happens if the tickets-<sha> entry already exists. The code itself says 'Fast-moving ticket tips rarely hit cache'. If the tickets branch moves between the pre-step and the gate's own call, the gate builds and publishes a new tickets-<sha> snapshot (_build_publish_account takes accounting_lock). That build runs inside the llm_review step, which is bounded only by the 1200 s cap and not by a step timeout. The plan's own root cause names 316 ticket snapshots, so ticket-snapshot builds are the hot case.
scenarios: A ticket event lands on the tickets branch during diff_fetch. The gate's resolve_gate_handle pins a new tickets sha and builds tickets-<newsha> inside llm_review, with no review_step log and no step timeout.
A future accounting-lock stall of any kind on the ticket-snapshot publish still silently uses up the 1200 s cap, so AC2's 'each step before the LLM call has its own timeout' is only partly met.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Correct the 'gate's own first call' premise: list the gate's pre-LLM work inside the adapter (preflight, assemble_diff_context, carry-forward ticket-store read) and either bound and log those as named steps or state explicitly that they are excluded from AC2 and why.
evidence: Plan step 4: "the gate's own first call (CodeReviewRequest defaults)"
Plan step 3: "logs an llm_review start line before the adapter (that step stays under the per-review timeout)"

src/rebar/llm/workflow/gate_dispatch.py:391-403: produce_code_review_verdict runs _code_review_preflight, then _assemble_code_review_run, then _run_code_review_gate (where resolve_gate_handle is called, line 541).

gate_dispatch.py:441-470: assemble_diff_context(...) and _standing_findings(request), which calls carry_forward.standing_items(key, repo_root=...) (carry_forward.py:96 sidecar.latest_code_review_result).
Plan Context: "Hypotheses to test: waiting on the tickets-store lock; ..."
AC: "Each review step before the LLM call logs when it starts and has its own timeout well under 1200 s."
findings.finding: Step 4 calls resolve_gate_handle 'the gate's own first call', but the code-review gate does several pre-LLM steps before it. These are runner.preflight() in _code_review_preflight, assemble.assemble_diff_context(...), and _standing_findings → carry_forward.standing_items → sidecar.latest_code_review_result, which reads the ambient ticket store. All of these run inside adapter.code_review_decision, so under the plan they sit in the llm_review step, which has no step timeout or start log. The plan's own hypothesis list includes 'waiting on the tickets-store lock', and AC2 requires every pre-LLM step to have its own timeout. A ticket-store read that stalls in carry-forward would therefore still be silent until 1200 s.
scenarios: A ticket-store lock contention in sidecar.latest_code_review_result blocks the carry-forward read. Nothing is logged after the llm_review start line until the 1200 s cap, and the deploy deferral is used up again.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Register the llm_review adapter thread with ReviewScratch (submit it through the same thread-tracking path, with the per-review timeout as its bound) so the folder outlives every thread that reads it, and add a test that cancels the review during llm_review.
evidence: Plan step 5: 'on close the folder is removed at once if no step thread runs in it, else by the last thread as it returns'
Plan step 3: 'logs an llm_review start line before the adapter (that step stays under the per-review timeout)'
voter.py:277-286 and :237-246 run adapter.code_review_decision(diff_text, repo_root, ...) via asyncio.to_thread; app.py:357-360 wraps the whole review in asyncio.wait_for(timeout=review_timeout)
gate_dispatch.py:541 resolve_gate_handle(repo_root=request.repo_root), where repo_root is the scratch clone
findings.finding: ReviewScratch only tracks threads started through run_step. The llm_review step (adapter.code_review_decision, which runs _assert_reviewed_tree, git diff/scope assembly, and resolve_gate_handle(repo_root=<clone>) against the scratch clone) stays a plain asyncio.to_thread under the 1200 s per-review wait_for. When that timeout cancels the coroutine, ReviewScratch.close() sees no run_step thread and deletes the folder while the adapter thread is still reading it. That is the same `reviewbot-… No such file` failure the plan sets out to remove.
findings.location: Approach step 3 ('that step stays under the per-review timeout') and step 5 (ReviewScratch removal rule)
scenarios: A review times out at 1200 s inside the gate: the voter coroutine is cancelled, ReviewScratch.close() deletes the clone, and the still-running adapter thread fails with ENOENT on the clone
findings.suggested_fix: Give run_step an optional timeout (None = no step bound) and run the llm_review adapter call through ReviewScratch's tracked submission, so close() waits for it like any other step thread. Add a Testing bullet: cancel the review mid-adapter, and the clone persists until the adapter thread returns.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] In Approach step 1, state why this reconcile is still worth running given that on the box the entry set will almost always change during a 45-51 min walk, or make it conditional or cheaper (e.g. run it only when sweep_tmp/_drain_trash_held actually removed debris or bytes.total is missing/unreadable), and add a test for the skipped-reset path under concurrent publishes.
evidence: Plan: 're-take it and reset the byte total only if the entry set is unchanged. Otherwise ... keep the incremental total.'
Plan Root cause: 'on the box the walk takes 45-51 minutes (316 ticket snapshots of ~224,000 files)'
gate_source.attach_materialized_tickets publishes a tickets-<sha> entry and calls gc_trigger.maybe_gc on each attested resolution
janitor.start_background_janitor runs startup_sweep() at every container start
findings.finding: The unlocked sweep keeps the walk's result only if no entry was published or evicted during the walk. On the box the walk lasts 45-51 minutes and the container restarts on roughly hourly deploys. During that window reviews keep publishing code and tickets-<sha> entries (316 ticket snapshots already exist), and gc_trigger.maybe_gc can evict. So the walked total will almost always be thrown away: the reconcile still costs about 45 minutes of full-store I/O per container start (alongside the 93 git maintenance timeouts) but rarely corrects anything. The plan gives no reason why a reconcile that almost never applies is worth that cost, and it does not consider a cheaper or conditional reconcile.
scenarios: A container starts after a deploy and a review publishes a new tickets-<sha> during minute 10 of the walk: the reset is skipped, so any drift stays, and the 45-minute I/O load was spent for nothing
Hourly deploys mean the walk runs for most of each container's life

Plan Context hypothesis: 'waiting on the tickets-store lock'

That work is runner preflight, assemble_diff_context (git plus scope-intent ticket resolution from trailers), _standing_findings (sidecar.latest_code_review_result reads the ticket store), _assert_reviewed_tree (git), and the ticket-store materialization half of resolve_gate_handle. This leaves the plan's own 'waiting on the tickets-store lock' hypothesis outside any step bound.
scenarios: A review blocks in the carry-forward ticket-store read: no step line appears after 'llm_review' starts, and the review runs to the 1200 s cap with the same silent signature as on 11-21

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Replace the entry-set check in startup_sweep with a generation counter bumped inside add_bytes_held (or justify the home-made token against the seqlock pattern and close its inode-reuse ABA gap)
evidence: Plan: "record the entry set (name + directory inode) in the same hold; walk with the lock released; re-take it and reset the byte total only if the entry set is unchanged"
janitor.py:198-218 _evict renames to trash and rmtrees under accounting_lock, which frees the directory inode for reuse; repo_snapshot.py:731-745 publishes a new directory under the same lock
cache.py:178-181 distinct_bytes skips files whose lstat fails, so a walk that overlaps an eviction undercounts without any error

Seqlock prior art: writers increment a sequence number under the lock and readers compare it before and after, retrying when it differs (retrieved: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seqlock, docs.kernel.org/locking/seqlock.html)
findings.finding: Approach step 1 invents its own token to check whether the store changed during the unlocked walk (the entry set of name + directory inode). The standard pattern for an optimistic read checked afterwards is a sequence/generation counter that writers bump while holding the lock (seqlock). The plan does not consider it. The home-made token has an ABA gap: if an entry is evicted (rename to trash + rmtree) and the same SHA is published again during the 45-51 minute walk, the new directory can reuse the old inode number. The entry set then looks unchanged, even though the walk saw half-gone files (lstat errors are skipped) and the incremental total already moved under the lock. The sweep would then overwrite a correct total with a wrong one.
scenarios: Container start runs the sweep. During the walk the GC evicts tickets-<sha>, a review then rebuilds that same SHA, and the filesystem hands out the freed directory inode again. The entry set compares equal, and the walk's partial count overwrites the correct incremental total.
findings.suggested_fix: Keep a generation counter next to bytes.total (for example a bytes.gen file written atomically in add_bytes_held, which every populate, eviction and drain already calls while holding accounting_lock). The sweep reads the counter under the first hold, walks without the lock, then re-takes the lock and resets the total only if the counter is unchanged. Add a test where an evict-then-republish of the same SHA happens mid-walk and the total must stay incremental.
